Furstenberg-Katznelson theorem (a+tF⊆A)

Words: 76
Additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
The multidimensional Szemerédi theorem says that a subset A⊆Zd with positive upper density contains a translated positive integer dilate a+tF of every finite set F⊆Zd. In the finite formulation, for every α>0 and finite F, all sufficiently large integer boxes have this property for every subset occupying at least an α fraction of the box. The one-dimensional case for F={0,1,…,r−1} is the Szemerédi theorem. The general result follows from multiple recurrence for commuting measure-preserving transformations.

Bracket-linear frequency function (θ(h)=β{γh}(mod1))

Words: 65
Additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
A frequency function built from an affine variable and its fractional part. Irrational γ and β can give many exact additive relations because each pair sum has only two possible floor carries. For example β=3​, γ=2​ gives ≫N3 additive quadruples on [−N,N], but agreement with every ordinary affine function occurs on only o(N) shifts. Integer floor points underlying affine agreement must be collinear.

Four-term progression hypergraph encoding (Li​=∑j=i​(j−i)xj​)

Words: 56
Additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
Use four parts indexed by 0,1,2,3 in a cyclic group G, and include the triple missing part i when Li​∈A. A transversal three-uniform tetrahedron then has the four values S1​−iS0​, where S0​=∑j​xj​ and S1​=∑j​jxj​, so it encodes a four-term arithmetic progression. Constant progressions give ∣A∣∣G∣2 edge-disjoint tetrahedra. This is the bridge from the tetrahedron removal lemma to the Szemerédi theorem.

Roth theorem on three-term arithmetic progressions

Words: 407 Articles: 4
Additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
For every δ>0, every sufficiently long integer interval has a nonconstant three-term arithmetic progression in each subset of subset density at least δ. This is a theorem about additive combinatorics, distinct from the Roth theorem on approximation of algebraic irrational numbers. The Roth density-increment step proves it by repeatedly increasing subset density on a shorter arithmetic progression.

Roth density increment on an integer progression (∣P∣≥cδ2N​,δP​≥δ+cδ2)

Words: 84
Roth theorem on three-term arithmetic progressions OurBigBook.com
If a density-δ subset of a sufficiently long integer interval has no nonconstant three-term arithmetic progression, Fourier expansion of the progression count gives a large coefficient of its balanced indicator. Dirichlet approximation supplies a step at most N​ on which that character varies slowly. Partitioning the interval into equal-length progressions of that step, and controlling the short tails, produces the displayed density increment. Iteration must terminate since density cannot exceed one. The same argument treats the three-point pattern with coefficients 2,−3,1.

Triangle-removal proof of Roth theorem

Words: 116
Roth theorem on three-term arithmetic progressions OurBigBook.com
Embed A⊆[N] in the odd cyclic group G=Z/(2N+1)Z, so additive three-term relations in A cannot wrap around. Form three copies of G, putting edges x∼y when y−x∈A, y∼z when z−y∈A, and x∼z when (z−x)/2∈A. A triangle in a graph encodes a+b=2c in A. If A has no nonconstant arithmetic progression, every triangle in a graph has a=b=c; there are exactly ∣G∣∣A∣ triangles in a graph, and they are edge-disjoint. Thus at least ∣G∣∣A∣ edges must be removed to eliminate them. For fixed positive subset density of A, this is a positive fraction of the squared vertex count, whereas the triangle in a graph count is only quadratic. The triangle removal lemma permits deletion of an arbitrarily small quadratic fraction when the cubic triangle in a graph subset density is sufficiently small. This contradiction establishes Roth theorem on three-term arithmetic progressions.

Classical Roth bound for three-term progressions (r3​(N)≪N/loglogN)

Words: 130
Roth theorem on three-term arithmetic progressions OurBigBook.com
Write r3​(N) for the maximum cardinality of a subset of [N] containing no nonconstant three-term arithmetic progression. There is an absolute constant C such that every three-term-progression-free subset A⊆[N] satisfies ∣A∣≤CN/loglogN for N≥3. A quantitative Roth density-increment step gives, for subset density δ and N≥4⋅106δ−4, a arithmetic progression of length at least δ2N​/2000 and increased subset density at least δ+δ2/64. The increment decreases reciprocal subset density by at least 1/65, so fewer than ⌈65/δ⌉ iterations are possible. If Nj​ is the successive length, then logNj+1​≥21​logNj​−log(2000/δ2), using the initial subset density to bound all later ones. Hence logNj​≥2−jlogN−2log(2000/δ2). If δloglogN exceeds a sufficiently large absolute constant, all these intervals remain above the density increment threshold, a contradiction. This proves the displayed bound. The result is a classical quantitative version of Roth theorem on three-term arithmetic progressions, without asserting an optimal bound.

High-energy Roth theorem

Words: 31
Roth theorem on three-term arithmetic progressions OurBigBook.com
For fixed θ>0, a sufficiently large finite set of integers with additive energy at least θ∣A∣3 has a nonconstant three-term arithmetic progression. The Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers theorem and Ruzsa modelling lemma reduce the problem to the Roth theorem on three-term arithmetic progressions in a dense cyclic model.

Product set (A⋅B)

Words: 149 Articles: 2
Additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
The product set of two sets of real numbers is A⋅B={ab:a∈A,b∈B}. It is a multiplicative counterpart of a sumset, not the Cartesian product A×B.

Multiplicative energy (E(A,B))

Words: 121 Articles: 1
Product set OurBigBook.com
For finite sets of nonzero real numbers, the multiplicative energy is the number of quadruples (a,b,c,d)∈A×B×A×B satisfying a/b=c/d. Swapping b,d shows that it also counts quadruples with ab=cd. Thus E(A,B)=∑x​rA⋅B​(x)2, where rA⋅B​(x) counts product representations. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality yields E(A,B)≥∣A∣2∣B∣2/∣A⋅B∣.

Multiplicative energy sumset bound (E(A,B)≤4⌈log∣B∣⌉∣A+A∣∣B+B∣)

Words: 70
Multiplicative energy OurBigBook.com
For finite sets of positive real numbers A,B with ∣B∣≥2, E(A,B)≤4⌈log∣B∣⌉∣A+A∣∣B+B∣, with natural or binary logarithm. Partition ray occupancies of A×B into ⌈log∣B∣⌉ classes of multiplicative width e, or width 2 for the binary convention. Injectivity of sums on two distinct rays and disjoint open planar sectors bound each class's sum of squared occupancies by 4∣A+A∣∣B+B∣. A singleton class contributes at most ∣A∣∣B∣. Combining this with the energy lower bound gives a sum-product inequality.

Corner in an integer grid ({(x,y),(x,y+d),(x+d,y)},d=0)

Words: 91 Articles: 1
Additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
A corner consists of these three points in the integer grid, all contained in the set being studied. The displacement may be positive or negative, but must be nonzero, so the points are distinct. The corners theorem guarantees a corner in every subset of positive fixed density of a finite subset of a sufficiently large square grid.

Corners theorem

Words: 42
Corner in an integer grid OurBigBook.com
For every δ>0, all sufficiently large integers n have the property that every A⊆[n]2 with ∣A∣≥δn2 contains a corner in an integer grid. The tripartite graph encoding of a grid turns the absence of a corner into a family of many edge-disjoint triangles but only quadratically many total triangles in a graph, contradicting the triangle removal lemma.

Cut norm (∥H∥cut​=maxA,B​∣EH1A​1B​∣)

Words: 56
Additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
For a real-valued function H on a nonempty finite Cartesian product X×Y, its normalized cut norm is the maximum of ∣Ex,y​H(x,y)1A​(x)1B​(y)∣ over A⊆X,B⊆Y. It measures all rectangular subset discrepancies. The convention using arbitrary test functions bounded by one is equivalent within a factor of four, by decomposing their positive and negative parts into indicator functions.

Non-abelian additive combinatorics

Words: 633 Articles: 13
Additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
Non-abelian additive combinatorics studies product sets and configuration counts in noncommutative groups. Fourier analysis on a finite group and quasirandom groups connect small-dimensional group representations with multiplicative mixing.

Matrix-valued Gowers U2 quantity (∥f∥U24​=Exy−1zw−1=e​tr(f(x)f(y)∗f(z)f(w)∗))

Words: 189 Articles: 2
Non-abelian additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
For f:G→Mn​(C) on a finite group, use uniform expectation over the solutions of xy−1zw−1=e and the ordinary, unnormalized trace to define the displayed fourth-order quantity. If Tρ​ is its matrix Fourier block, this quantity equals ∑ρ​dρ​Tr((Tρ​Tρ∗​)2), so it is real and nonnegative. For a scalar function on an abelian group, it reduces to the usual fourth power of the Gowers uniformity norm of order two. The unnormalized trace means a unitary matrix-valued function can have fourth-order quantity as large as n.

Spectral inverse theorem for the matrix-valued U2 quantity (cn/2≤∑p​dρp​​≤2n/c)

Words: 56
Matrix-valued Gowers U2 quantity OurBigBook.com
If ∥f(x)∥op​≤1 and ∥f∥U24​≥cn>0, select the singular values λp​≥c/2​ of the matrix Fourier blocks. Their weighted count m=∑p​dρp​​ lies between cn/2 and 2n/c. Scaling unit right singular vectors and their corresponding unit left singular vectors by dρp​​​ gives matrices U(p),V(p) satisfying Ex​f(x)U(p)ρp​(x)∗=λp​V(p) and Hilbert-Schmidt inner product orthogonality within each chosen irreducible representation. The Schur averaging of rectangular matrices then gives Ex​∥UP(x)∗b∥22​=∥b∥22​ for the concatenated U and the corresponding block diagonal matrix P(x).

Words: 56
Matrix-valued Gowers U2 quantity OurBigBook.com
For f:G→Mn​(C) and a degree-dρ​ unitary irreducible representation, the matrix Fourier block is the operator Tρ​ on Mn×dρ​​(C) defined in the title. Its singular values λρ,j​ satisfy
∑ρ,j​dρ​λρ,j2​=Ex​∥f(x)∥HS2​,∑ρ,j​dρ​λρ,j4​=∥f∥U24​.
(1)
Pointwise operator norm at most one implies ∥Tρ​∥op​≤1. These blocks are operators on a matrix space, rather than simply the entrywise scalar Fourier transform on a finite group without any reshaping.

Quasirandom group (dρ​≥m for ρ=1)

Words: 89 Articles: 1
Non-abelian additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
A finite group is m-quasirandom if every nontrivial irreducible representation over the complex numbers has degree at least m. The trivial representation is excluded. Large m suppresses correlations of products of arbitrary subsets, through product mixing in a quasirandom group.

Product mixing in a quasirandom group (∥f∗g∥2​≤m−1/2∥f∥2​∥g∥2​)

Words: 60
Quasirandom group OurBigBook.com
For an m-quasirandom group, uniform expectations, and the normalized convolution on a finite group, a scalar mean-zero function f satisfies
∥f∗g∥2​≤m−1/2∥f∥2​∥g∥2​.
(2)
The Fourier analysis on a finite group proof bounds each nontrivial matrix component of f in operator norm using its weighted Hilbert-Schmidt norm. For subsets of subset density values a,b,c, the error in their normalized product count is at most a(1−a)b(1−b)c(1−c)/m​. In particular abc>1/m guarantees a solution of xy=z in the three subsets.

Words: 337 Articles: 7
Non-abelian additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
For a finite group, choose one unitary irreducible representation ρ of degree dρ​ from each equivalence class. One consistent normalized Fourier transform on a finite group convention is f​(ρ)=Ex​f(x)ρ(x). The Schur orthogonality relations give
f(x)=∑ρ​dρ​tr(f​(ρ)ρ(x)∗),Ex​∣f(x)∣2=∑ρ​dρ​∥f​(ρ)∥HS2​.
(3)
The normalized convolution on a finite group satisfies f∗g​(ρ)=f​(ρ)g​(ρ) in this convention. Using ρ(x)∗ in the transform instead reverses that product order for scalar functions with the same normalized convolution on a finite group convention. The Fourier transform on a finite group has matrix-valued components even when the original function is scalar-valued.

Fourier analysis on a finite group OurBigBook.com
For a scalar function on a group, use (Ra​f)(x)=f(xa) as the right-translation convention. For Fourier analysis on a finite group this gives Ra​f​(ρ)=f​(ρ)ρ(a)∗. Specifying whether a or a−1 appears in the definition avoids sign and multiplication-order ambiguity.

For a scalar function on a group, left translation by a is (La​f)(x)=f(a−1x). With the positive-representation convention for Fourier analysis on a finite group, La​f​(ρ)=ρ(a)f​(ρ).

Fourier transform on a finite group (f​(ρ)=Ex​f(x)ρ(x))

Words: 128 Articles: 2
Fourier analysis on a finite group OurBigBook.com
For a scalar function on a finite group, one normalized transform convention assigns the matrix Ex​f(x)ρ(x) to each chosen unitary irreducible representation. This map is a weighted Hilbert space isomorphism by the Parseval identity on a finite group. Another common convention uses ρ(x)∗; the corresponding convolution theorem on a finite group then reverses the matrix product order for (f∗g)(x)=Ey​f(y)g(y−1x).

Words: 42
Fourier transform on a finite group OurBigBook.com
For the Fourier transform on a finite group, the displayed identity uses uniform expectation in the original function space and a weighted Hilbert-Schmidt inner product in the matrix components. In particular ∥f∥22​=∑ρ​dρ​∥f​(ρ)∥HS2​. For an abelian group, all dρ​=1, and the identity becomes a sum of squared scalar coefficients.
Fourier inversion on a finite group (f(x)=∑ρ​dρ​tr(f​(ρ)ρ(x)∗))
Words: 39
Fourier transform on a finite group OurBigBook.com
The Fourier transform on a finite group convention f​(ρ)=Ex​f(x)ρ(x) has the displayed inversion formula. The sum is over one representative from each equivalence class of unitary irreducible representations. It follows from the Schur orthogonality relations and the regular representation decomposition, and holds at every group element without a limiting argument.

Normalized convolution on a finite group ((f∗g)(x)=Ey​f(y)g(y−1x))

Words: 85 Articles: 1
Fourier analysis on a finite group OurBigBook.com
For scalar functions on a finite group, normalized convolution on a finite group is (f∗g)(x)=∣G∣−1∑y​f(y)g(y−1x). It is associative and need not commute. Its identity is ∣G∣1{e}​, rather than the unscaled indicator function of the identity element. The Fourier analysis on a finite group convention f​(ρ)=Ef(x)ρ(x) turns it into matrix multiplication in the same order.

Words: 40
Normalized convolution on a finite group OurBigBook.com
The normalized convolution on a finite group and the Fourier transform on a finite group convention with ρ(x) satisfy the displayed identity. Substitute x=yz in the defining expectation and use ρ(yz)=ρ(y)ρ(z). With the convention using ρ(x)∗ instead, the scalar convolution has transform g​(ρ)f​(ρ); multiplication order matters for noncommutative groups.

Box norm (∥f∥□​)

Words: 597 Articles: 8
Additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
For nonempty finite sets X,Y and a function f:X×Y→C on their Cartesian product, using uniform expectations, define
∥f∥□4​=Ex,x′,y,y′​f(x,y)f(x′,y)​f(x,y′)​f(x′,y′).
(4)

Then E∣U∣≥ρn and Eb(U)≤τn2. Some y has ∣U∣−16b(U)/(ρn)≥ρn/2, so ∣U∣≥ρn/2 and b(U)≤∣U∣2/8. Remove vertices with more than ∣U∣/4 bad partners. At least half remain. A product that cancels constant phases and lowers the degree of a polynomial phase. For f(x)=e(αx2), it is e(2αhx+αh2). The Gowers uniformity norm derivative identity relates a higher norm to the average of lower norms of these derivatives.

Quadratic uniformity of a set (∥1A​−∣A∣/∣G∣∥U3​≤α)

Words: 280 Articles: 2
Gowers U3 norm OurBigBook.com
A subset A of a finite abelian group G with subset density η=∣A∣/∣G∣ is quadratically α-uniform, in the norm convention, if its balanced subset indicator g=1A​−η has Gowers U3 norm at most α. This controls correlations on additive three-dimensional cubes after the subset density contribution is removed. If a convention instead bounds the eighth power of the norm by α, its parameter corresponds to the norm parameter α1/8. The convention must therefore be stated when giving quantitative thresholds.
Four-term progressions in a quadratically uniform interval set (α≪δ32⟹Λ4​(1A​)>diagonal count)
Words: 93
Quadratic uniformity of a set OurBigBook.com
Balance the indicator by its density on the interval, and extend it by zero to a cyclic group of order greater than twelve times the interval length and coprime to six. An eighth-power interval cube bound α bounds every four-term counting error by α1/8 through three Cauchy–Schwarz steps. The density contribution is bounded below by a constant times δ4, and the diagonal contribution tends to zero with interval length. A sufficiently small constant times δ32 therefore guarantees a nonconstant four-term progression. Stating the cube normalization distinguishes this parameter from the norm convention.
Triangular weights count genuine four-term progressions (weighted count≥η4t4−4⋅61/8αt2)
Words: 122
Quadratic uniformity of a set OurBigBook.com
For A⊆ZN​, N≥16, put η=∣A∣/N, M=⌊N/16⌋, J={0,…,M−1}, and w=1J​∗1J​ using normalized convolution on a finite group. The weights w(x)w(d−M) are supported where 0≤x≤2M−2 and M≤d≤3M−2, so x,x+d,x+2d,x+3d are distinct integer points below N. If t=M/N, then Ew=t2 and the sum of absolute values of its Fourier coefficients is t, by Parseval identity on a finite group. Expanding the four indicators around their subset density leaves four terms with one balanced factor. Expand both weights in Fourier series and absorb each character e(rx+sd) into the factors at x and x+d. Character multiplication preserves the Gowers U3 norm, and the cyclic four-term progression bound with torsion factors bounds every error by 61/8α. Thus the weighted count is at least η4t4−4⋅61/8αt2. Since t≥1/32, positivity follows from α<η4/(4096⋅61/8).

Unbounded torsion obstructs uniform control of four-term progressions (∥f∥U3​→0 ⇒ Λ4​→0 uniformly in G)
Words: 103
Four-term progression bound with torsion factors OurBigBook.com
A bound tending to zero with one factor's Gowers U3 norm, uniformly over all finite abelian groups, is false. On G=F2m​, choose a random independent sign at each point. A cube with eight distinct vertices has sign product of expectation zero. The probability of a collision among its vertices is at most (28​)/∣G∣, since each equality of distinct vertices imposes a nonzero linear equation in the increments. Thus some sign function f has ∥f∥U38​≤28/∣G∣. But the four-term arithmetic progression is (x,x+d,x,x+d), so choosing factors (f,1,f,1) gives correlation identically one. As m→∞, the norm tends to zero. Bounded torsion, as in cyclic groups, avoids this obstruction.

Gowers U3 norm on an interval (∥f∥U3(N)​)

Words: 57
Gowers U3 norm OurBigBook.com
Normalize the conjugated cube average by the number of integer cubes whose vertices all lie in the interval. Equivalently, extend f by zero to a cyclic group of order greater than 8N and divide its Gowers U3 norm by that of the interval's indicator function. A quadratic phase then has norm one. Omitting the denominator gives a different but uniformly equivalent interval normalization.

Inverse theorem for the Gowers U3 norm over a finite field OurBigBook.com
If a dense set has too few four-term arithmetic progressions, its balanced function has large U3 norm. Freiman lifting of a progression
Words: 65
Freiman s-isomorphism OurBigBook.com
An eight-term Freiman isomorphism extends injectively to the two-sum/two-difference set by sending its representations to the corresponding integer differences. Independence of representation uses four-term relations, and additivity whenever y,z,y+z lie in that difference set uses six-term relations. Thus a proper symmetric progression in the modeled difference set lifts, one coordinate step at a time, to a proper integer progression of the same rank and cardinality.
Freiman 2-isomorphism (a1​+a2​=a3​+a4​⟺ϕ(a1​)+ϕ(a2​)=ϕ(a3​)+ϕ(a4​))
Words: 124 Articles: 1
Freiman s-isomorphism OurBigBook.com
A Freiman 2-isomorphism is a bijection between subsets of abelian groups preserving additive quadruple relations in both directions. It need not extend to an ambient group homomorphism. Multiplication by a nonzero scalar in a finite field and translation are examples; reduction of an integer set modulo a prime is an example only when it creates no new additive relations.
Minimal binary Freiman models have full fourfold sumset (4A=F2m​,2m≤K4∣A∣)
Words: 75
Freiman 2-isomorphism OurBigBook.com
If a Freiman 2-isomorphism into F2m​ uses minimal m, every nonzero vector lies in the fourfold sumset. Otherwise quotienting by the line it spans would preserve all additive quadruple relations and would still be injective, contradicting minimality. Since zero also belongs to the fourfold sumset, that sumset is the full model group. Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality then bounds its size by K4∣A∣. A finite subset of the direct sum of countably many binary fields has a finite-dimensional model to start with.

Ruzsa modelling lemma

Words: 494 Articles: 4
Freiman s-homomorphism OurBigBook.com
The Ruzsa modelling lemma says that a finite set with bounded doubling has a large subset Freiman s-isomorphic to a dense subset of a finite cyclic group, whose order is bounded by a constant depending only on the doubling constant and s times the original set size.
Cardinality-controlled cyclic Freiman model (∣A′∣≥∣A∣/(k+1),N=4∣kA−kA∣+1)
Words: 98
Ruzsa modelling lemma OurBigBook.com
A nonempty finite integer set has a subset of the displayed size Freiman s-isomorphic to a subset of ZN​. Embed in a sufficiently large auxiliary prime modulus and randomly dilate. Avoid the residues of every nonzero multiple of N of absolute value less than that prime for all nonzero members of kA−kA; a union bound gives a successful dilation. Retain a most-populated one of k+1 short intervals of representatives. Its k-term sum differences have absolute value less than the auxiliary prime, so reduction modulo N both preserves and reflects relations. Under ∣kA−kA∣≤C∣A∣, this gives N≤4C∣A∣+1.

Ruzsa modelling lemma OurBigBook.com
For ∣A+A∣≤K∣A∣, one can take q=8∣8A−8A∣≤8K16∣A∣. Embed in a much larger prime cyclic group and choose a dilation avoiding the residues of all nonzero multiples of q of absolute value below that prime for every nonzero eightfold difference. A union bound ensures such a dilation. Retain a most-populated ninth-interval of representatives. Eight-term sums then have range shorter than the prime, and reduction modulo q both preserves and reflects eight-term additive relations.
Half-size prime cyclic Freiman model (∣A′∣≥∣A∣/2,p>4K4∣A∣)
Words: 274 Articles: 1
Ruzsa modelling lemma OurBigBook.com
For a nonempty integer set with doubling constant at most K, Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality bounds ∣2A−2A∣ by K4∣A∣. Embed the set modulo a sufficiently large auxiliary prime q, randomly dilate it, and select the more populated of two half-intervals of representatives. Differences of two pair sums on that half have absolute value less than q, so the lift preserves original relations. Every nonzero original difference is uniformly dilated among nonzero residues; avoiding all residues represented by nonzero multiples of p of absolute value less than q has positive probability when p>4∣2A−2A∣. Reduction modulo p then yields a Freiman 2-isomorphism on the selected half.
Half-size cyclic Freiman model with a sharp difference-set bound (N>∣2A−2A∣⟹∣A′∣≥∣A∣/2)
Words: 175
Half-size prime cyclic Freiman model OurBigBook.com
For a finite nonempty integer set A, put D=2A−2A. If an integer N>∣D∣, some A′⊆A of size at least ∣A∣/2 has a Freiman 2-isomorphism into Z/NZ. Choose an auxiliary prime P>N so large that reduction is injective on A and every nonzero element of D remains nonzero. Dilate modulo P by a uniformly chosen nonzero multiplier. The forbidden residues are those represented by nonzero multiples of N of absolute value less than P, at most 2⌊(P−1)/N⌋ residues. The nonzero elements of D occur in opposite pairs; the two elements in each pair have the same bad event. The union bound therefore gives failure probability at most (∣D∣−1)/N<1. Choose a multiplier avoiding all these events. Select the more populated of two half-intervals of residues modulo P. Differences of two pair sums of representatives then have absolute value less than P. An original additive relation must therefore lift to equality in the integers; conversely an equality modulo N cannot have a nonzero lifted difference, by the forbidden-residue choice. Reduction modulo N is the required isomorphism.

An abelian progression is a generalized arithmetic progression inside an abelian group. It is the image of an integer box under a group homomorphism.
